title: You're Taking Your Creatine Wrong — Thomas DeLauer
text: You're Taking Your Creatine Wrong — Thomas DeLauer You're Taking Your Creatine Wrong Thomas DeLauer · Nutrition & Performance · youtu.be/V8-Iz9ofDRY Mind Map Full Summary Actionable Takeaways You're Taking Your Creatine Wrong — Thomas DeLauer Timing Mistakes Pre-Workout Myth Most people take creatine only pre-workout believing it gives an immediate energy boost. Creatine doesn't work acutely — it must saturate muscle cells over days. Consistent daily dosing matters far more than precise timing around training. Post-Workout Window Research suggests post-workout may be slightly superior due to increased insulin sensitivity and muscle cell permeability after exercise. This window allows creatine to be taken up more efficiently alongside a carb-protein meal. Fasted Dosing Error Taking creatine on an empty stomach without any carbohydrates reduces insulin-mediated uptake into muscle cells. Insulin acts as a transport enhancer — pairing creatine with even a small amount of carbohydrates meaningfully improves cellular delivery. Consistency Over Precision The single biggest timing mistake is inconsistency. Skipping days drops intramuscular stores. Pick a consistent daily time — even off-training days — and stick to it. Saturation is the goal, not peak levels at any single moment. Loading Phase Errors Skipping the Load Skipping a loading phase means it takes 3–4 weeks of 3–5g daily to reach full muscle saturation. A loading protocol (20g/day split 4×5g for 5–7 days) saturates stores in one week — faster performance benefits and less wasted time. Mega-Loading Mistake The other extreme is taking excessive doses (10g+ at once) thinking more is better. Large single doses simply get excreted via the kidneys. The body can only absorb ~3–5g at once effectively. Split large daily doses into multiple servings. Maintenance Miscalculation After loading, many drop to too low a maintenance dose. For larger athletes or those with higher muscle mass, 5g/day may still be suboptimal. Body weight matters — some individuals need 0.1g per kg of lean body mass to maintain saturation. Cycling Off Unnecessarily Cycling off creatine is an outdated practice with no scientific basis. Your body doesn't downregulate creatine transporters meaningfully with supplementation. Stopping only requires a rebuild period. Continuous use is both safe and more effective. Hydration & Form Under-Hydration Creatine pulls water into muscle cells (cell volumization). Without increased fluid intake, this can leave you dehydrated elsewhere, causing cramping and fatigue. Increase daily water by at least 500ml when starting or loading creatine. Choosing the Wrong Form Creatine HCl and Kre-Alkalyn are marketed as superior but research consistently shows creatine monohydrate to be the gold standard. It has the most human research, the highest bioavailability when dissolved fully in water, and the lowest cost per effective dose. Undissolved Powder Creatine monohydrate doesn't dissolve easily in cold water. Undissolved particles pass through the gut less effectively. Use warm water and stir thoroughly, or mix with a warm beverage. This simple step meaningfully improves actual absorption. Mixing with Caffeine Older studies suggested caffeine may interfere with creatine's ergogenic effects, though evidence is mixed. As a precaution, avoid mixing creatine directly in high-caffeine pre-workouts — take them at different times or use caffeine-free hydration with your creatine dose. Diet Pairing Errors No Carbohydrate Co-Ingestion Insulin is a key driver of creatine transport into muscle cells via GLUT transporters. Consuming creatine with 30–50g of fast-digesting carbohydrates (dextrose, white rice, fruit) can increase muscular uptake by up to 60% compared to creatine alone. Keto / Low-Carb Conflict Low-carb dieters miss the insulin-creatine synergy entirely. Pairing creatine with leucine or a protein-rich meal can partially compensate via protein-stimulated insulin release, though not as powerfully as carbohydrate co-ingestion. High-Fiber Interference Taking creatine with very high-fiber foods slows gastric emptying and may reduce the speed of uptake. For optimal delivery, take creatine with low-fiber, easily digestible carbohydrates rather than with high-fiber whole foods. Brain & Beyond Ignoring Cognitive Benefits Most people think of creatine as purely a muscle supplement. Research shows creatine supports brain phosphocreatine stores, improving working memory, mental fatigue resistance, and cognitive performance — especially under sleep deprivation or stress. Wrong Dose for Brain Cognitive benefits may require slightly higher doses than muscle performance (some studies use 10–20g/day for acute brain effects). DeLauer notes that for cognitive support, consistency and potentially higher maintenance dosing matters more than it does for athletic gains. Overlooking Vegetarians Vegetarians and vegans have significantly lower baseline muscle creatine stores since dietary creatine comes primarily from meat and fish. They respond more dramatically to supplementation — both in performance and cognitive measures — making creatine especially important for this group. Why Most People Get Creatine Wrong Thomas DeLauer opens by addressing one of the most persistent myths in fitness nutrition: that creatine works like a pre-workout stimulant that needs to be taken right before training for maximum effect. In reality, creatine's mechanism is entirely different — it saturates intramuscular phosphocreatine stores over multiple days, and the acute timing of any single dose matters far less than consistent daily intake. The common practice of only dosing on training days and skipping rest days actively undermines the purpose of supplementation. Loading Protocols and Saturation DeLauer explains the logic behind loading phases: the goal is to reach full muscle saturation as quickly as possible. A standard loading protocol of 20g per day (split across four 5g doses) for 5–7 days achieves in one week what would take nearly a month with low-dose maintenance-only approaches. However, he cautions against excessive single doses — the body can only absorb around 3–5g at a time effectively, and anything beyond that is largely excreted by the kidneys. After loading, a maintenance dose adjusted to body mass (roughly 0.1g per kilogram of lean mass) sustains full stores indefinitely with no need to cycle off. The Role of Insulin and Carbohydrate Pairing One of the most impactful and under-appreciated aspects of creatine supplementation is its interaction with insulin. Insulin activates creatine transporters (primarily SLC6A8) on muscle cell membranes, dramatically increasing how much creatine enters cells versus remains in circulation. Taking creatine alongside 30–50g of fast-digesting carbohydrates triggers an insulin spike that can increase cellular uptake by up to 60% compared to taking creatine with water alone. For keto or low-carb followers, leucine-rich protein is a partial substitute since protein itself stimulates modest insulin secretion. Hydration, Form, and Dissolution Cell volumization — the pulling of water into muscle cells — is one of creatine's key mechanisms for enhancing strength and cell signaling. This makes proper hydration non-negotiable. DeLauer recommends increasing daily water intake by at least 500ml when starting or during a loading phase. On form selection, he is direct: creatine monohydrate backed by decades of human research outperforms every marketed alternative at a fraction of the cost. The one practical step most people miss is ensuring the powder is fully dissolved, ideally in warm water, as undissolved creatine particles absorb less efficiently through the gut wall. Cognitive and Broader Health Benefits DeLauer emphasizes that most people leave significant benefit on the table by thinking of creatine as purely a muscle supplement. The brain is highly energy-demanding and maintains its own phosphocreatine pool, which creatine supplementation can augment. Studies show improvements in working memory, reaction time, and resistance to cognitive fatigue — effects that are particularly pronounced in sleep-deprived states and among vegetarians who begin with depleted baseline stores. The case for daily creatine, DeLauer argues, is as much about cognitive longevity as it is about athletic performance. Takeaway 01 Take creatine every single day — including rest days. Consistency of saturation beats perfect workout-day timing every time. Takeaway 02 Use a loading phase (4×5g daily for 5–7 days) if you want full performance benefits within a week rather than 3–4 weeks. Takeaway 03 Never take more than 5g in a single dose during maintenance — the excess is excreted. Split larger doses throughout the day. Takeaway 04 Always pair your creatine dose with 30–50g of fast carbohydrates (fruit juice, white rice, dextrose) to maximize insulin-driven uptake into muscle. Takeaway 05 Dissolve creatine monohydrate in warm water before drinking — undissolved granules absorb less effectively through the intestinal wall. Takeaway 06 Increase your daily water intake by at least 500ml when supplementing — creatine pulls water into cells and can dehydrate you without it. Takeaway 07 Choose creatine monohydrate over expensive alternatives — it has the most research, highest proven bioavailability, and lowest cost per dose. Takeaway 08 If you eat low-carb, pair creatine with a leucine-rich protein source to partially compensate for the lack of carb-driven insulin response. Takeaway 09 Take creatine for brain health, not just muscle — daily supplementation supports memory, cognitive endurance, and mental performance under fatigue. Takeaway 10 If you're vegetarian or vegan, prioritize creatine supplementation — your baseline stores are significantly lower and your response will be more dramatic than meat-eaters.

title: Increase Creatine Uptake by 30% — Thomas DeLauer
text: Increase Creatine Uptake by 30% — Thomas DeLauer Increase Creatine Uptake by 30% Thomas DeLauer · Nutrition & Performance · youtu.be/W4K8OT0nmfI Mind Map Full Summary Actionable Takeaways Increase Creatine Uptake by 30% — Thomas DeLauer Insulin as the Master Key SLC6A8 Transporter Activation Creatine enters muscle cells primarily through the SLC6A8 (CRT1) sodium-dependent transporter. Insulin signaling directly upregulates the activity and membrane expression of this transporter, creating a biochemical window of dramatically enhanced uptake immediately after carbohydrate ingestion. The 30% Uptake Window Studies comparing creatine taken with simple carbohydrates versus water alone show 30–60% greater retention in muscle tissue. The effect is driven by the insulin spike that follows carbohydrate digestion — the higher and faster the insulin response, the more creatine gets transported into cells before circulating levels clear. Optimal Carb Amount Research points to 30–50g of fast-digesting carbohydrates as the sweet spot. Dextrose (pure glucose) produces the sharpest insulin spike. Alternatives include white rice, banana, fruit juice, or sports drinks. More carbohydrates beyond this threshold don't appear to linearly increase uptake further. Protein + Carb Synergy Combining protein with carbohydrates produces a greater insulin response than carbohydrates alone due to the insulinogenic effect of amino acids (particularly leucine). DeLauer recommends taking creatine with a post-workout shake containing both fast carbs and a complete protein source for maximal transport. Sodium & Cell Swelling Sodium-Dependent Transport The CRT1 creatine transporter is sodium-dependent — it co-transports sodium ions alongside creatine molecules. Adequate sodium levels in the extracellular fluid are therefore necessary for efficient creatine uptake. Low sodium intake may limit transport rate even when creatine and insulin are both present. Cell Volumization Feedback As creatine enters muscle cells, it draws water in via osmosis (cell volumization). This swelling itself acts as an anabolic signal — cells detect the hydration increase and upregulate protein synthesis pathways and reduce protein breakdown. The uptake and the benefit are mutually reinforcing. Electrolyte Balance DeLauer suggests ensuring adequate electrolyte intake — particularly sodium and potassium — when supplementing creatine. Coconut water, a lightly salted post-workout meal, or an electrolyte supplement alongside creatine can support the sodium gradient that powers the CRT1 transporter. Beta-Alanine Synergy Buffering Fatigue Together Beta-alanine raises intramuscular carnosine levels, which buffer the acidity (H+ ions) generated during high-intensity exercise. Creatine replenishes phosphocreatine for explosive energy. Together they address different rate-limiting factors of performance — combining them produces additive benefits neither achieves alone. Shared Timing Window Both creatine and beta-alanine are best taken with carbohydrates and around training. Taking them together in a post-workout carb-protein meal is efficient and may allow synergistic improvements in sustained high-intensity work output — the type most responsive to both compounds. Dosing Considerations Effective beta-alanine dosing is 3.2–6.4g daily, often split to reduce the tingling (paresthesia) side effect. Unlike creatine, there is no established loading protocol — accumulation is gradual. DeLauer notes the combination is particularly effective for athletes doing repeated bouts of 60–240 second high-intensity work. Exercise-Induced Uptake Post-Exercise Sensitivity Resistance exercise increases muscle glucose and creatine transporter density and sensitivity for 1–2 hours post-workout. Muscle cell membranes are more permeable, glycogen resynthesis is occurring, and insulin sensitivity is elevated — making the immediate post-workout window the most effective time to ingest creatine. Phosphocreatine Depletion Signal During intense exercise, muscle phosphocreatine stores are substantially depleted. This depletion itself signals upregulated creatine transporter expression — the muscle is biochemically primed to restock. Supplementing immediately after training capitalizes on this active transport upregulation. Practical Post-Workout Stack DeLauer's recommended stack: 5g creatine monohydrate + 30–50g fast carbs + 20–30g protein within 30 minutes post-training. This hits insulin, amino acid, and sodium transport mechanisms simultaneously at the moment of peak muscle cell receptivity. What Blocks Uptake Caffeine Interference High caffeine intake may antagonize some of creatine's intracellular effects. While current evidence is mixed, DeLauer recommends separating a caffeine-heavy pre-workout from your creatine dose by at least 30–60 minutes, and avoiding mixing creatine directly into high-stimulant pre-workout blends. Already-Saturated Stores Once muscles are fully saturated, additional creatine simply cannot enter cells regardless of insulin levels or timing strategy. This is why a proper loading phase is valuable — reaching saturation quickly, then shifting to a maintenance dose to keep stores full without wasteful overconsumption. Gut Absorption Limits Large single doses overwhelm gut absorption capacity. GI distress — bloating, cramping, loose stools — is a sign that creatine is fermenting in the gut rather than absorbing into the bloodstream. Splitting doses (3–5g maximum per sitting) in warm water eliminates this issue entirely. The 30% Uptake Principle Thomas DeLauer opens this video with a bold but research-backed claim: most people are absorbing significantly less creatine than they could be, not because of poor product quality, but because of what they take it with. The 30% figure comes from controlled studies comparing creatine retention in muscle tissue when taken with versus without carbohydrates. The mechanism is insulin — the hormone that acts as a master key for creatine's primary cellular transporter, SLC6A8 (CRT1). The Insulin-Creatine Transport Mechanism The CRT1 transporter is sodium-dependent and insulin-responsive. When blood insulin rises following carbohydrate ingestion, CRT1 expression and activity at the cell membrane increases dramatically. The result is a window of elevated creatine influx into muscle cells that doesn't exist when the same dose is taken with plain water. DeLauer explains that 30–50g of fast-digesting carbohydrates — dextrose, fruit juice, white rice — is sufficient to trigger a meaningful insulin response. Adding protein creates a further synergistic effect since amino acids, especially leucine, independently stimulate insulin secretion through the mTOR pathway. Sodium, Electrolytes, and Cell Swelling A less discussed but mechanistically important factor is sodium. The CRT1 transporter is sodium co-dependent — sodium ions are transported alongside creatine molecules, meaning low sodium status actively limits transport rate. DeLauer points out that athletes who sweat heavily and eat low-sodium diets may be inadvertently throttling their creatine uptake regardless of dosing strategy. Adequate electrolyte intake — sodium, potassium, and magnesium — supports the electrochemical gradient that powers the transporter. Once creatine enters the cell, osmotic water follows, causing the characteristic muscle fullness of creatine loading. This cell swelling itself acts as an anabolic signal. The Post-Workout Window and Beta-Alanine Stack Exercise substantially increases creatine transporter sensitivity and cell membrane permeability. Phosphocreatine depletion during training triggers upregulated CRT1 expression as the muscle prepares to restock. DeLauer argues that the 30–60 minute post-workout window is therefore the single highest-leverage moment for creatine ingestion — combining the exercise-induced receptor upregulation with an insulin-stimulating carb-protein meal creates conditions for maximum uptake. He also covers the practical synergy with beta-alanine, which addresses a different rate limiter (muscular acidosis during sustained effort), making the combination more effective than either supplement alone for high-intensity athletes. What Prevents Optimal Uptake DeLauer closes by cataloguing the main uptake blockers: taking creatine on an empty stomach, using caffeine-heavy pre-workouts in the same dose window, taking large single doses that overwhelm gut absorption, and attempting to supplement into already-saturated muscle stores. The practical prescription is simple — load properly to reach saturation, then maintain with 5g post-workout paired with carbohydrates and protein, ensure adequate hydration and electrolyte intake, and avoid the common mistake of mixing creatine into high-caffeine pre-workouts. Takeaway 01 Always take creatine with 30–50g of fast-digesting carbohydrates to activate insulin-driven CRT1 transporter expression and increase uptake by up to 30%. Takeaway 02 Add 20–30g of protein to your creatine dose — the leucine content amplifies the insulin response beyond what carbohydrates produce alone. Takeaway 03 Take creatine within 30 minutes post-workout when phosphocreatine depletion peaks and CRT1 transporter expression is at its highest. Takeaway 04 Maintain adequate sodium intake — the CRT1 transporter is sodium co-dependent and low sodium limits transport rate regardless of insulin levels. Takeaway 05 Use electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium) alongside creatine supplementation — especially if you sweat heavily or eat low-sodium. Takeaway 06 Stack creatine with beta-alanine (3.2–6.4g/day) if you do repeated high-intensity efforts lasting 60–240 seconds — they address different fatigue mechanisms. Takeaway 07 Never exceed 5g of creatine in a single dose — more overwhelms gut absorption capacity and causes GI distress without additional benefit. Takeaway 08 Separate creatine from your caffeine intake by at least 30–60 minutes to avoid potential antagonism of creatine's intracellular effects. Takeaway 09 Complete a loading phase before trying to optimize uptake timing — no strategy overcomes unsaturated stores, and loading gets you to full saturation in a week. Takeaway 10 Practical post-workout stack: 5g creatine + 40g fast carbs + 25g protein in warm water — this combination hits every known transport-enhancement mechanism at once.

title: Thomas DeLauer — Perfect Fasting Length: Muscle, Fat Loss & Brain | Mind Map
text: Thomas DeLauer — Perfect Fasting Length: Muscle, Fat Loss & Brain | Mind Map Thomas DeLauer · YouTube · 2026 Study Discovers Perfect Fasting Length for Muscle, Fat Loss Brain Benefits Thomas DeLauer — Science-Backed Nutrition Performance 4M+ YouTube subscribers · Author, Intermittent Fasting Made Easy 🧠 Mind Map 📖 Full Summary ⚡ Takeaways Tap any branch to expand · Tap a leaf for detail 🔬 What the Study Actually Found ▼ A multi-outcome analysis of fasting windows ▶ The study DeLauer references assessed fasting periods across a spectrum — from short overnight fasts (12 hours) through extended fasts (24–72+ hours) — measuring simultaneous effects on skeletal muscle structure, fat oxidation, and markers of brain health. Most prior research had optimised for only one outcome at a time; this research attempted to find the duration at which all three benefit curves peak simultaneously. MRI and MRS — measuring muscle in real time ▶ The research used 31P and 1H magnetic resonance spectroscopy alongside MRI to assess skeletal muscle energy metabolism and structural changes during fasting — non-invasive techniques that can track ATP turnover, phosphocreatine stores, lipid infiltration, and glycogen depletion in living tissue without biopsies. This provides a more accurate window into what actually happens inside muscle during a fast than indirect blood markers alone. The convergence point — where all three peak ▶ The research identified a window — approximately 16 to 18 hours for most metabolically healthy individuals — where fat oxidation is running at a high rate, ketone production is sufficient to fuel the brain and produce cognitive benefits, autophagy has been meaningfully initiated, and muscle protein breakdown has not yet crossed into a net-catabolic state. Beyond this window, the trade-offs begin to accumulate. Before it, some benefits (particularly brain and autophagy) haven't fully activated. Individual variation matters ▶ DeLauer emphasises that the "perfect" length is not a single universal number. Metabolically healthy, lean, active individuals tend to shift into fat-burning more quickly and can tolerate longer fasts with less muscle catabolism. Individuals with insulin resistance, higher body fat, or sedentary lifestyles may reach the same metabolic states at different timings. The study's "optimal window" is a population average — your personal window may shift based on metabolic health, training status, and glycogen levels going into the fast. Why this matters beyond weight loss ▶ DeLauer frames this study as cutting through the noise around fasting protocols. The fasting conversation is often dominated by fat loss as the primary metric. This research provides evidence that properly timed fasts have compounding effects — on autophagy (cellular recycling), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), mitochondrial biogenesis, and inflammation reduction — that extend well beyond body composition and represent meaningful healthspan interventions. ⏱️ What Happens at Each Fasting Stage ▼ 0–6 hours: fed state, digestion running ▶ After a meal, insulin is elevated and the body is in an anabolic, glucose-burning state. Liver glycogen stores are replenishing and blood glucose is being distributed to tissues. Fat oxidation is minimal during this window — the body has no reason to reach into fat stores when glucose is plentiful. This is why simply skipping breakfast provides limited fasting benefit if dinner was late. 6–12 hours: glycogen depletion begins ▶ As blood glucose falls and insulin drops, the liver begins breaking down glycogen to maintain blood sugar. By around 10–12 hours of fasting for most people, liver glycogen is substantially depleted. The body starts increasing fat oxidation and the respiratory quotient shifts — more fat, less glucose, is being burned. This is the transition window most people pass through during a normal overnight fast. 12–16 hours: the metabolic switch ▶ This is what DeLauer calls the "metabolic switch" — the transition from primarily glucose to primarily fat as fuel. Ketone production begins to climb meaningfully. Growth hormone pulses start increasing (GH rises significantly to protect lean mass during fasting). Norepinephrine rises, mobilising fat from adipose tissue. The brain begins receiving a growing proportion of its fuel from beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) rather than glucose. 16–24 hours: peak benefit window ▶ Fat oxidation is running at a high rate. Ketones are elevated enough to measurably fuel the brain and suppress appetite. Autophagy — the cellular recycling process that clears damaged proteins and organelles — has been meaningfully upregulated. Growth hormone is elevated, providing a muscle-protective signal. BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) levels are rising. For most people, this is where the maximum benefit-to-cost ratio sits: significant metabolic improvements with manageable muscle-preservation risk. 24–72+ hours: extended fasting trade-offs ▶ Beyond 24 hours, autophagy continues to deepen and cortisol begins rising more significantly to mobilise fuel. The body starts breaking down muscle protein at a faster rate for gluconeogenesis — producing glucose from amino acids. Growth hormone remains elevated but cannot fully offset catabolic pressure. These longer fasts have therapeutic uses (particularly for autophagy, immune reset, and potentially cancer prevention) but carry meaningful muscle-loss risk for active individuals without careful protein refeeding strategies. 🎯 The 16–18 Hour Sweet Spot ▼ Why 16–18 hours hits all three targets ▶ At 16–18 hours, fat oxidation is running at near-peak rates, ketone production is sufficient to deliver meaningful brain benefits (BHB at ~0.5–1.5 mmol/L for most people), autophagy is meaningfully active, and GH is elevated enough to maintain a muscle-protective environment. The body has not yet entered the more aggressively catabolic territory of multi-day fasting. This window captures most of the benefit curve before the cost curve rises steeply. Fat loss mechanism — why it works beyond calories ▶ DeLauer emphasises that the fat loss effect of properly timed fasting goes beyond simple caloric restriction. The combination of low insulin, elevated glucagon, high catecholamines, and activated hormone-sensitive lipase creates a hormonal environment specifically suited to mobilising stored fat — particularly visceral adipose tissue, which is more sensitive to adrenergic stimulation than subcutaneous fat. This is why fasting can preferentially reduce visceral fat even when total caloric deficit is equivalent to non-fasting approaches. Autophagy — not just a weight-loss bonus ▶ Autophagy is the process by which cells identify, tag, and recycle damaged proteins, dysfunctional organelles, and misfolded structures. DeLauer frames it as the body's internal quality-control and deep-cleaning system. Properly functioning autophagy reduces the buildup of cellular debris linked to neurodegeneration, cancer risk, and accelerated aging. At 16–18 hours, autophagy is meaningfully active — particularly in the liver and neurons — making this window genuinely beneficial beyond aesthetics. Growth hormone — fasting's muscle insurance policy ▶ GH rises substantially during fasting — by as much as 2–5x over baseline in some studies — and serves as the body's primary muscle-preservation signal during caloric restriction. GH promotes fat mobilisation while opposing muscle protein breakdown, effectively telling the body to spare lean tissue and burn stored fat instead. This GH surge is one of the key reasons a 16–18 hour fast preserves muscle much more effectively than a 16-hour caloric deficit spread across the whole day. Sustainability — the protocol you can actually maintain ▶ A 16–18 hour fast is typically achieved by eating within an 6–8 hour window during the day — for example, noon to 7pm. For most people, this means skipping breakfast, which is a manageable daily adjustment rather than a dramatic lifestyle disruption. DeLauer's argument is that the best fasting protocol is one that generates meaningful benefits while being sustainable enough to maintain consistently, since the compounding benefits of regular fasting far outweigh the marginal gains of occasional extreme fasts. 💪 Muscle Preservation During Fasting ▼ The gluconeogenesis concern — when does it matter? ▶ Gluconeogenesis — the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources including amino acids — does occur during fasting. However, within a 16–18 hour fast, the primary substrates for gluconeogenesis are lactate, glycerol (from fat breakdown), and alanine from muscle. DeLauer explains that the GH surge and ketone availability at this duration substantially reduce the demand for muscle-derived amino acids as fuel, keeping net muscle catabolism minimal for most healthy individuals. Resistance training supercharges muscle retention ▶ Training within the feeding window sends a powerful anabolic signal that primes muscle for preservation even during the subsequent fast. Resistance training increases insulin sensitivity in muscle tissue specifically, meaning that when you do eat, nutrients are preferentially directed toward muscle. DeLauer recommends timing resistance training to fall within or just before the eating window — not in the deep fasting period — to maximise the mTOR activation that follows feeding. Protein quality and timing at breaking the fast ▶ How you break the fast matters as much as the fast itself for muscle preservation. DeLauer emphasises leucine-rich protein sources at the first meal — whey, eggs, or high-quality animal protein — because leucine is the primary amino acid trigger for mTOR activation and muscle protein synthesis. A meal providing 30–50g of quality protein with sufficient leucine (at least 2.5–3g) provides a robust anabolic signal that can compensate for the mildly catabolic fasting period and produce a net-positive muscle protein balance for the day. The mTOR–autophagy balance ▶ mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin) and autophagy are inversely related: when mTOR is high (fed, anabolic state), autophagy is suppressed; when mTOR is low (fasted state), autophagy activates. DeLauer argues this is actually a feature, not a bug: the fasting window activates autophagy and cellular cleaning, while the eating window activates mTOR, protein synthesis, and muscle building. Cycling between these states — rather than keeping one perpetually active — appears to be the biological design for optimal body composition and longevity. What breaks autophagy vs what breaks the fast ▶ DeLauer addresses the common confusion around what breaks a fast versus what breaks autophagy. Black coffee, plain tea, and electrolytes with no caloric content do not meaningfully spike insulin and do not break the fasted state for most metabolic purposes, including fat oxidation. Autophagy, however, is more sensitive: even small amounts of protein or branched-chain amino acids can begin to suppress it. For pure autophagy maximisation, the fast needs to be truly calorie-free; for fat loss and general health benefits, the rules are somewhat more permissive. 🧠 Brain Benefits — Why Fasting Makes You Sharper ▼ BDNF — the brain's own growth factor ▶ Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a protein that supports the growth, maintenance, and connectivity of neurons. It is closely associated with learning, memory, mood regulation, and protection against neurodegeneration. Fasting has been shown to increase BDNF levels in animal models and shows promising signals in human studies — with the effect appearing to kick in most strongly in the 14–20 hour fasting range. Higher BDNF is associated with better cognitive performance, lower depression risk, and slower neurological aging. Ketones as premium brain fuel ▶ Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) and acetoacetate, the primary ketone bodies produced during fasting, cross the blood-brain barrier and provide the brain with an efficient, clean-burning fuel source. Unlike glucose metabolism, ketone oxidation produces fewer reactive oxygen species, meaning less oxidative stress on neurons. DeLauer describes ketones as "neuroprotective" — they have been studied for their potential therapeutic role in conditions from Alzheimer's disease to traumatic brain injury, and their acute effects on mental clarity and focus are consistently reported by those who fast regularly. Reduced neuroinflammation ▶ Chronic neuroinflammation is a feature of virtually every major neurodegenerative disease. Fasting-induced ketosis reduces the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and inhibits the NLRP3 inflammasome — a key driver of neuroinflammation. BHB specifically has been shown to act as an endogenous inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome, providing an anti-inflammatory effect that operates independently of caloric restriction itself. This is one reason why both fasting and ketogenic diets have been studied for conditions like Alzheimer's, epilepsy, and multiple sclerosis. Mental clarity in the fasted state — why it happens ▶ The subjective experience of heightened mental clarity during fasting is well-documented anecdotally and has plausible physiological explanations. Elevated norepinephrine sharpens attention and alertness. Stable blood sugar (rather than the spikes and crashes of frequent feeding) prevents the cognitive dips associated with post-meal insulin responses. Ketones provide a steady, efficient fuel stream to the brain. And the suppression of mTOR during fasting shifts cellular resources toward repair and maintenance — including neuronal housekeeping — rather than growth, which may contribute to the clarity many people report. Autophagy in neurons — a specific brain benefit ▶ Neurons are particularly long-lived cells that accumulate damaged proteins and dysfunctional organelles over time. Unlike most cells, neurons cannot simply divide and replace damaged ones — they depend heavily on autophagy for maintenance. DeLauer frames neuronal autophagy during fasting as one of the most underappreciated brain health interventions available: clearing the debris that, when allowed to accumulate, contributes to the plaques and tangles associated with Alzheimer's and other neurodegenerative conditions. Regular fasting keeps this housekeeping process running efficiently. 🛠️ Practical Implementation ▼ The 16:8 starting point — keep it simple ▶ For most people, a 16-hour fast with an 8-hour eating window is the most practical entry point. In concrete terms: stop eating by 8pm, skip breakfast, and eat your first meal at noon. You sleep through 8 of those fasting hours, making the actual waking fast only about 4 hours. DeLauer emphasises that consistency matters more than precision — a 15-hour fast done reliably every day produces better compounding results than a 24-hour fast done occasionally. Electrolytes — the overlooked fasting essential ▶ As insulin drops during fasting, the kidneys excrete sodium and other electrolytes at a higher rate — a process that accelerates the further into the fast you go. Headaches, fatigue, brain fog, and muscle cramps during fasting are almost always electrolyte depletion, not "detox" or hunger. DeLauer recommends sodium (from a quality source like Himalayan salt or electrolyte supplements), magnesium, and potassium to be maintained throughout the fasting window. This alone resolves most of the side effects people attribute to fasting difficulty. Coffee — accelerates the fast's benefits ▶ Black coffee during the fasting window is not just permissible — it may actively enhance the fast's benefits. Caffeine increases fat oxidation by stimulating norepinephrine and upregulating hormone-sensitive lipase. Chlorogenic acids in coffee improve insulin sensitivity. And there is evidence that caffeine may have a mild autophagy-inducing effect on its own. DeLauer's position: black coffee in the fasting window accelerates the metabolic shift and can make the fast easier to maintain without compromising its core benefits. How to break the fast for maximum benefit ▶ Breaking the fast well matters enormously for body composition. DeLauer's protocol: begin with a small amount of protein and fat (not a large carbohydrate load) to gently signal the body out of the fasted state without an insulin spike. After 15–20 minutes, follow with a proper protein-rich meal. Avoid ultra-processed foods as the first meal, since the gut is more permeable during fasting and the first nutrients absorbed have outsized effects on metabolic signalling for the remainder of the day. Who should approach fasting carefully ▶ DeLauer consistently flags that fasting is not universally appropriate. Those with a history of disordered eating, pregnant or breastfeeding women, individuals with type 1 diabetes or on blood-glucose-lowering medications, those who are underweight, and people under significant physiological stress (illness, major surgery recovery) should approach fasting with medical guidance. The benefits are real and significant — but they don't override individual physiology or medical circumstances, and the research context is important to understand. 🔬 What the Research Says Thomas DeLauer breaks down a study examining fasting windows across a wide duration spectrum — from standard overnight fasts through extended multi-day fasts — measuring simultaneous effects on skeletal muscle structure, fat oxidation rates, and markers of brain health. What makes this research distinctive is its attempt to find the duration at which benefits across all three domains peak concurrently, rather than optimising for any single outcome. Using techniques including magnetic resonance spectroscopy and MRI to assess muscle energy metabolism in living tissue, the study provides a more direct window into what actually happens inside the body during different fasting lengths than previous research had achieved. The core finding DeLauer emphasises: there is a convergence zone — approximately 16 to 18 hours for most metabolically healthy individuals — where fat oxidation is running at a high rate, ketone production is sufficient to meaningfully fuel and protect the brain, autophagy has been initiated, and muscle protein breakdown has not yet escalated into a net-catabolic state. This window shifts based on individual metabolic health, training status, and glycogen stores going into the fast — leaner, more metabolically flexible individuals tend to enter this zone earlier. ⏱️ The Metabolic Timeline of a Fast DeLauer walks through what actually happens in the body hour by hour. In the first 6 hours after eating, insulin is elevated and the body is burning glucose — fat oxidation is minimal. Between 6 and 12 hours, liver glycogen depletes progressively and fat oxidation begins climbing. The "metabolic switch" — the transition from primarily glucose to primarily fat as fuel — occurs at roughly 12–16 hours for most people. Growth hormone begins pulsing higher to protect lean mass. Ketone production climbs noticeably. Norepinephrine rises, mobilising fat from adipose tissue. The brain begins receiving a growing proportion of its fuel from beta-hydroxybutyrate rather than glucose. Between 16 and 24 hours, the body is in its peak benefit zone. Fat oxidation is high, ketones are elevated enough to measurably suppress appetite and support brain function, autophagy is meaningfully active, GH is elevated, and BDNF levels are rising. Beyond 24 hours, cortisol begins climbing more substantially, gluconeogenesis from muscle amino acids accelerates, and the catabolic pressure on lean tissue grows. Extended fasts (48–72+ hours) have specific therapeutic applications — deep autophagy, immune system reset — but carry meaningful muscle-loss risk for active individuals and require careful refeeding strategies. 💪 Muscle: The Surprising Non-Problem The most common objection to fasting for active people is muscle loss.
