title: Thomas De Lauer – 1 Scoop Fades Wrinkles, Brightens Skin and Reverses Biological Aging
text: Thomas De Lauer – 1 Scoop Fades Wrinkles, Brightens Skin and Reverses Biological Aging Thomas De Lauer – 1 Scoop Fades Wrinkles, Brightens Skin Reverses Biological Aging Thomas De Lauer • YouTube • June 2026 • Brain Cognitive Health | Nutrition Longevity 🧠 Mind Map 📄 Full Summary ✅ Actionable Takeaways ✨ Collagen: The "1 Scoop" Explained ▶ What Collagen Peptides Are ▶ Collagen peptides are hydrolysed collagen — broken into smaller amino acid chains (primarily glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline) that are easily absorbed through the gut wall. Unlike intact collagen, these peptides can enter the bloodstream and signal fibroblasts in the dermis to upregulate native collagen production. Why Collagen Declines With Age ▶ After the mid-20s, the body produces approximately 1% less collagen per year. Cumulative UV exposure, high sugar intake (which causes glycation of collagen fibres), smoking, and chronic inflammation all accelerate this decline. By age 40, the skin's structural scaffolding has measurably thinned, causing visible wrinkles and reduced elasticity. The Fibroblast Signalling Mechanism ▶ Ingested collagen peptides — particularly the dipeptide prolyl-hydroxyproline (Pro-Hyp) — are detected by fibroblasts in the skin's dermis. These cells respond by increasing synthesis of Type I and Type III collagen, hyaluronic acid, and elastin. This makes oral collagen supplementation a true upstream signalling intervention, not just a protein source. Clinical Evidence for Wrinkle Reduction ▶ Multiple randomised controlled trials with 2.5–10g of hydrolysed collagen daily for 8–12 weeks show statistically significant improvements in skin hydration, elasticity, and wrinkle depth. A 2019 meta-analysis confirmed these effects across multiple populations, with benefits appearing as early as 4 weeks of consistent daily supplementation. ✨ ▶ Glycine and Antioxidant Synthesis ▶ Glycine, collagen's most abundant amino acid, is a precursor to glutathione — the body's master antioxidant. Higher glutathione levels reduce oxidative stress in skin cells, combating the reactive oxygen species that cause dullness, hyperpigmentation, and uneven tone. Supplementing collagen thus indirectly boosts the skin's intrinsic brightening chemistry. Hyaluronic Acid Stimulation ▶ Collagen peptide supplementation stimulates fibroblasts to co-produce hyaluronic acid, which binds up to 1000x its weight in water. Well-hydrated skin cells are plumper, light-scattering more uniformly, creating the luminous, "lit from within" appearance that tracks as skin brightness to the human eye and in imaging studies. Melanin Modulation ▶ Some research suggests collagen-derived peptides can modulate melanocyte activity — the cells responsible for melanin (pigment) production. Reduced oxidative stress in melanocytes leads to more uniform, regulated pigment distribution, reducing the appearance of age spots and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation that accumulate through sun and environmental damage. Barrier Function Restoration ▶ Collagen supplementation improves the integrity of the skin barrier — the outermost layer of cells that retains moisture and excludes irritants. A stronger barrier prevents transepidermal water loss (TEWL), which is the primary driver of dull, lacklustre skin. Improved barrier function is measurable within weeks using corneometric devices. 🕰️ Biological Age Reversal — The Claims ▶ What "Biological Age" Means ▶ Biological age, unlike chronological age, measures how old your cells and tissues actually function. Tools like DNA methylation clocks (Horvath, GrimAge) quantify epigenetic ageing patterns. Thomas De Lauer references this concept to argue that collagen and associated lifestyle interventions can measurably shift these markers in a younger direction. Collagen's Role in Cellular Senescence ▶ Degraded extracellular matrix — of which collagen is the primary component — is now understood to promote cellular senescence (the "zombie cell" state where cells stop dividing but remain metabolically active, secreting pro-inflammatory compounds). Maintaining matrix integrity through collagen supplementation may reduce the senescent cell burden over time. Systemic Anti-Inflammatory Effects ▶ Glycine has demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects in multiple contexts — inhibiting NF-kB signalling and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine output. Since chronic inflammation ("inflammageing") is now understood as the primary driver of biological ageing across all tissues, collagen's glycine load provides systemic benefits beyond skin that could measurably affect ageing biomarkers. Nuance: Reversal vs. Slowing ▶ De Lauer is careful to note that "reversal" in biological ageing terms refers to shifting measurable biomarkers — methylation clocks, inflammatory markers, skin structure — rather than literally reversing time. The science supports that these markers can move in a younger direction, but the magnitude and durability depend heavily on complementary lifestyle practices. 💊 Optimising Collagen Supplementation ▶ Dose and Type That Works ▶ Research-backed dosing is 2.5–10g of hydrolysed collagen peptides daily. Type I collagen (from bovine or marine sources) is most studied for skin. Marine collagen has slightly smaller peptide sizes, potentially improving absorption. Grass-fed bovine collagen (such as that from Bubs Naturals) provides a clean source with predictable amino acid profiles. Vitamin C as a Cofactor ▶ Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for the enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine residues during collagen synthesis — without it, collagen cannot be properly formed in the body. De Lauer recommends pairing collagen supplementation with vitamin C (100–200mg) to ensure the body can actually utilise the ingested peptides for new collagen construction. Timing and Absorption ▶ Collagen can be consumed any time of day, but some research supports fasted or pre-exercise consumption. Taking it before exercise may increase collagen synthesis in connective tissue by driving blood flow to tendons and ligaments. For pure skin benefits, consistency of daily intake matters far more than specific timing windows. What Blocks Collagen Effectiveness ▶ High sugar diets accelerate collagen glycation — cross-linking collagen fibres in a way that makes them rigid and dysfunctional. Smoking depletes vitamin C and generates oxidative stress directly at the skin level. Excess alcohol impairs liver function and nutrient absorption. Addressing these blockers amplifies the benefit of supplementation significantly. 🏃 Lifestyle Stack That Amplifies Results ▶ Sleep as the Master Regulator ▶ Growth hormone — which peaks during deep sleep — is the primary endogenous signal for collagen synthesis throughout the body. Chronic sleep deprivation not only reduces growth hormone output but elevates cortisol, which actively degrades collagen. De Lauer emphasises that no supplement compensates for consistently poor sleep when targeting skin and biological age. Resistance Training and Collagen Synthesis ▶ Resistance exercise creates mechanical stress on connective tissue, triggering collagen synthesis in muscles, tendons, and to some extent skin. When combined with collagen supplementation (pre-workout), multiple studies show enhanced tendon and ligament collagen deposition compared to supplementation or exercise alone — a clear synergistic effect. Sun Protection as Preservation ▶ UV radiation is the single largest driver of collagen degradation and skin biological ageing — responsible for up to 80% of visible facial ageing. SPF use is therefore the highest-leverage skin intervention per unit of effort. De Lauer frames supplementation and sun protection as complementary: build new collagen and stop the primary thing destroying it. Fasting and Autophagy ▶ Intermittent fasting, a cornerstone of De Lauer's broader framework, promotes autophagy — the cellular recycling process that clears damaged proteins and organelles. Autophagic clearance of glycated, cross-linked collagen fibres creates space for newly synthesised collagen to organise properly. This makes fasting a structural complement to collagen supplementation. 📊 De Lauer's Evidence Framework ▶ How He Evaluates Supplements ▶ Thomas De Lauer applies a hierarchy of evidence to supplementation claims: randomised controlled trials carry the most weight, followed by mechanistic studies, then observational data. He explicitly distinguishes between in-vitro (cell culture), animal, and human studies, reserving strong recommendations for interventions with multiple human RCTs showing consistent effects. Partnership Transparency ▶ The video includes a paid partnership with Bubs Naturals, a collagen supplement brand. De Lauer acknowledges this explicitly. He notes that he only partners with brands whose products align with the scientific evidence he covers — but audiences should weigh sponsored content with appropriate scepticism while still evaluating the underlying science independently. Individualisation Matters ▶ De Lauer consistently frames outcomes as population averages rather than guarantees. Response to collagen supplementation varies by baseline collagen status, gut absorption efficiency, complementary nutrient status (especially vitamin C), and lifestyle factors. He recommends tracking progress through skin photos, subjective hydration perception, and joint discomfort levels over 8–12 weeks. The Compound Effect Argument ▶ De Lauer's central thesis is not that collagen alone reverses ageing but that it is a high-leverage addition to a comprehensive protocol. Collagen + vitamin C + sleep + resistance training + sun protection + reduced sugar creates a compound effect where each element amplifies the others — the biological age reversal claim rests on this stack, not on any single intervention. The Central Claim: One Supplement, Multiple Skin Mechanisms Thomas De Lauer, a health optimisation expert and prolific YouTube educator, presents hydrolysed collagen peptides as the "one scoop" capable of fading wrinkles, brightening skin, and shifting biological age markers. The video is built on a layered mechanistic argument: collagen peptides, once absorbed, signal fibroblasts in the skin's dermis to upregulate native collagen, hyaluronic acid, and elastin production. This is not simply a protein supplement — it is a signalling molecule that triggers the body's own regenerative machinery. The clinical evidence across multiple randomised controlled trials supports measurable improvements in wrinkle depth, skin hydration, and elasticity after 8–12 weeks of daily supplementation at doses of 2.5–10g. Why Skin Brightening Is a Real, Mechanistic Effect The brightening claim rests on several converging mechanisms. Glycine — collagen's most abundant amino acid — serves as a precursor to glutathione, the body's master antioxidant. Higher glutathione levels reduce oxidative stress in melanocytes, leading to more uniform pigment distribution and reduced age spots. Simultaneously, fibroblast-stimulated hyaluronic acid production increases cellular hydration, causing skin cells to scatter light more uniformly — the physical basis of luminous, healthy-looking skin. Improved barrier function further reduces transepidermal water loss, compounding the visible brightening effect through better moisture retention. Biological Age Reversal — The Scientific Framing De Lauer is careful with this claim. "Biological age reversal" refers to shifting measurable biomarkers — DNA methylation clocks, inflammatory markers, skin structural integrity — in a younger direction. The mechanism he focuses on is collagen's role in the extracellular matrix: degraded matrix promotes cellular senescence, while maintained matrix integrity supports normal cell cycling. Glycine's anti-inflammatory properties add a systemic dimension, as chronic low-grade inflammation ("inflammageing") is the underlying driver of accelerated biological ageing across all tissues. He presents collagen as one component of a broader anti-ageing stack rather than a standalone magic bullet. Optimising Supplementation: What Actually Works Research-backed dosing is 2.5–10g of hydrolysed collagen peptides daily, preferably paired with vitamin C (100–200mg) — an essential cofactor for collagen synthesis enzymes. Marine collagen has slightly smaller peptides and potentially better absorption than bovine, though both have strong evidence bases. De Lauer highlights key blockers: high-sugar diets (causing collagen glycation), smoking (depleting vitamin C), and alcohol (impairing nutrient absorption). Addressing these blockers can significantly amplify the benefit of supplementation, making dietary context as important as the supplement itself. The Lifestyle Stack: Where the Compound Effect Lives De Lauer's broader argument is about stacking: collagen supplementation produces the most meaningful biological age effects when layered onto adequate sleep (growth hormone-mediated collagen synthesis peaks during deep sleep), resistance training (mechanical stress on connective tissue synergises with supplementation), daily SPF use (UV is responsible for 80% of visible facial ageing), and intermittent fasting (autophagy clears glycated collagen fibres). No single intervention achieves the full effect — the compound protocol is the point, with collagen serving as one high-leverage, science-backed addition to it. 01 Start with 5g of hydrolysed collagen peptides daily. This sits in the middle of the 2.5–10g research range and is sufficient to trigger fibroblast signalling for measurable skin improvements in 8–12 weeks. 02 Always pair collagen with 100–200mg of vitamin C. Without this cofactor, your body cannot properly hydroxylate proline and lysine — the critical step in building functional collagen fibres from supplemented peptides. 03 Reduce daily sugar intake to below 25g added sugars. Glycation — sugar's cross-linking of collagen fibres — is one of the primary mechanisms of skin ageing and directly counteracts the benefit of collagen supplementation. 04 Apply SPF 30+ every morning, regardless of weather. UV radiation drives up to 80% of visible facial ageing through collagen degradation — sun protection is the highest-leverage skin intervention per unit of effort, bar none. 05 Prioritise 7–9 hours of sleep nightly. Growth hormone — the primary signal for collagen synthesis — peaks during deep sleep. No supplement compensates for chronically poor sleep when targeting skin quality and biological age. 06 Add resistance training 3x/week to amplify collagen deposition. Mechanical stress on connective tissue upregulates collagen synthesis, and when combined with pre-workout supplementation, the effect is synergistic — not additive. 07 Consider intermittent fasting to support autophagy. Autophagic clearance of glycated, damaged collagen fibres makes structural room for newly synthesised collagen to organise properly in the dermis. 08 Track your results with fortnightly photos in consistent lighting. Skin changes from collagen supplementation are gradual and easy to miss day-to-day — photo documentation over 8–12 weeks is the most reliable progress metric. 09 Choose hydrolysed (peptide) collagen over gelatin or whole collagen. Only hydrolysed peptides are small enough to be absorbed into the bloodstream and reach fibroblasts — the form matters as much as the dose. 10 Build the full stack: collagen + vitamin C + sleep + resistance training + SPF + low sugar. Biological age reversal is a compound effect — each element amplifies the others. The supplement alone produces a fraction of the outcome the full protocol achieves.

title: 2oz of This Replaces Your Entire Supplement Cabinet — Mind Map
text: 2oz of This Replaces Your Entire Supplement Cabinet — Mind Map Thomas DeLauer 2oz of This Replaces Your Entire Supplement Cabinet Published July 9, 2026 · NAD+ / Liposomal Delivery / Longevity Science Mind Map Full Summary Actionable Takeaways Why NAD+ Declines With Age ▶ The 50% age-related drop ▶ NAD+ levels fall by roughly half between age 20 and 60. DeLauer uses this decline as the central justification for the video: if a molecule this important is disappearing on a predictable curve, replenishing it becomes a maintenance issue rather than an optional upgrade. CD38 and PARP consumption ▶ NAD+ isn't just under-produced with age — it's actively consumed faster by enzymes like CD38 and the PARP family. This dual pressure (less made, more used) is why simply "eating better" rarely restores youthful NAD+ levels on its own. Downstream consequences ▶ A shrinking NAD+ pool doesn't stay isolated — it ripples into mitochondrial energy output, DNA repair capacity, and metabolic regulation simultaneously. DeLauer frames this as why NAD+ support can feel like it touches "everything" rather than one narrow symptom. Why precursors alone can fall short ▶ Popular precursors like NR and NMN do raise circulating NAD+, but they're subject to rapid consumption by CD38/PARPs and the body's own homeostatic feedback loops that cap how high levels climb. This is the setup DeLauer uses to argue for delivering NAD+ itself, rather than relying on the body to convert a precursor. How Liposomal Delivery Works ▶ The bioavailability gap ▶ Standard oral NAD+ or precursor capsules are estimated to reach only about 10–20% effective absorption, largely destroyed in the gut before they're useful. Liposomal formulations are marketed as pushing that figure toward 60%, which is the core selling point DeLauer builds the episode around. Phospholipid protection ▶ Liposomes are tiny spheres built from a phosphatidylcholine bilayer — the same material that makes up human cell membranes. Wrapping NAD+ inside this shell shields it from stomach acid and digestive enzymes so more of the molecule survives intact until it reaches circulation. Direct delivery vs. precursor conversion ▶ Rather than supplying a precursor and hoping the body's enzymatic machinery converts it efficiently, liposomal NAD+ delivers the finished molecule directly. DeLauer positions this as removing a conversion bottleneck that limits how much precursor-based supplementation actually raises NAD+. Why the liquid format matters ▶ A liquid liposomal suspension increases surface area contact in the mouth and gut compared to a capsule, and some absorption is believed to occur through lymphatic uptake that partially bypasses first-pass liver metabolism. This is presented as another reason the liquid delivery outperforms pills. Mitochondria Cellular Energy ▶ NAD+ as an electron carrier ▶ NAD+ shuttles electrons through the mitochondrial electron transport chain, a core step in producing ATP — the body's basic energy currency. Without an adequate NAD+ pool, this chain runs less efficiently, which DeLauer ties directly to the fatigue many people notice as they age. Fighting age-related fatigue ▶ Restoring NAD+ availability is framed as supporting mitochondrial respiration broadly, rather than acting as a stimulant. The pitch is that it addresses a root cause of low cellular energy output instead of masking tiredness the way caffeine does. Positioned upstream of other energy supplements ▶ DeLauer contrasts NAD+ with supplements like CoQ10 or creatine, arguing those support specific downstream energy processes while NAD+ acts further upstream as a rate-limiting cofactor for hundreds of enzymatic reactions, including energy metabolism. A complement to, not a replacement for, diet ▶ Even while pitching the product, the mitochondrial argument rests on NAD+ being a cofactor the body already uses constantly — meaning sleep, training load, and whole-food nutrition still set the ceiling on how much a supplement alone can move the needle. DNA Repair PARP Enzymes ▶ PARP1's outsized NAD+ appetite ▶ When DNA is damaged, the enzyme PARP1 activates and can consume up to 80% of the nuclear NAD+ pool to fuel repair. That single number illustrates how much cellular "budget" genomic maintenance can claim when NAD+ is scarce. The repair-depletion cycle ▶ DNA damage triggers PARP activation, which consumes NAD+; but NAD+ depletion has been shown to reduce DNA repair rates by up to 40%, creating a feedback loop where the very process meant to fix damage is starved of its fuel. DeLauer uses this to argue that low NAD+ compounds genomic aging rather than just slowing it. Genomic stability as an aging lever ▶ Accumulated, unrepaired DNA damage is one of the recognized hallmarks of cellular aging. Framing NAD+ support around PARP function ties the supplement to a mechanism deeper than "energy" — genomic maintenance itself. Balancing repair demand with sirtuin demand ▶ PARPs and sirtuins draw from the same NAD+ pool, so periods of high DNA-damage load (intense UV exposure, heavy training, illness) can starve sirtuin activity of substrate. This sets up the next branch's argument for keeping NAD+ levels high enough to fund both processes at once. Sirtuins Longevity Pathways ▶ Sirtuins need NAD+ as substrate ▶ Sirtuins such as SIRT1 are NAD+-dependent deacetylases — they cannot function without NAD+ as a direct co-substrate. Practically, this means no sirtuin activator (including resveratrol) can do anything in a cell whose NAD+ pool is already depleted. Resveratrol synergy ▶ Resveratrol works as an allosteric activator of SIRT1, increasing the enzyme's catalytic efficiency for whatever NAD+ concentration is available — it amplifies the effect of existing NAD+ rather than replacing the need for it. DeLauer uses this to make the case that NAD+ and sirtuin activators are complementary, not redundant, supplements. Cell viability and senescence ▶ Sirtuin activity is linked to reduced markers of cellular senescence and improved cell viability under stress. This is part of the broader "healthy aging" framing rather than a claim about lifespan extension in humans, where evidence remains preliminary. The "master switch" framing ▶ Sirtuins are often described as a master regulatory switch connecting metabolism, inflammation, and aging pathways. It's a useful mental model, but worth treating as a simplification — human longevity trials on sirtuin pathways are still limited compared to the mechanistic cell and animal data this framing leans on. Practical Dosing Stacking ▶ The daily serving ▶ The featured product (Rho Nutrition's Liposomal NAD+) is dosed at roughly 4ml per day — just under a teaspoon — delivering about 100mg of NAD+ per serving from a bottle sized for about 30 servings. Format and tolerability ▶ It's a vegan, sugar-free, keto-friendly liquid with a light lemon flavor, designed to avoid the GI discomfort some people report with high-dose NR or NMN capsules. Liquid liposomal formats are generally easier to titrate than fixed-dose pills. What it's pitched to replace ▶ DeLauer's core pitch is consolidation: instead of a cabinet of separate energy, longevity, and antioxidant pills, one liposomal liquid covers several of those bases at once. That's a convenience argument as much as a biochemical one, and worth weighing against simply taking the individual, cheaper components separately. Sponsor context ▶ This segment is a paid partnership with Rho Nutrition, promoted with the discount code DELAUER20. The underlying NAD+/liposomal science is real and published, but the specific product claims and "replaces your whole cabinet" framing come from a sponsored placement, not an independent review. Why NAD+ Declines With Age The episode opens from a simple but stark data point: NAD+ levels drop by roughly half between age 20 and 60. DeLauer explains that this isn't purely a production problem — enzymes like CD38 and the PARP family actively consume NAD+ faster as the body ages and accumulates cellular stress, so the pool shrinks from both ends at once. Because NAD+ feeds mitochondrial energy production, DNA repair, and metabolic signaling simultaneously, its decline is presented as a plausible common thread behind several unrelated symptoms of aging rather than a single, narrow deficiency. How Liposomal Delivery Works The central hook of the video is bioavailability: standard oral NAD+ and precursor supplements are estimated to reach only 10–20% effective absorption, while liposomal delivery is marketed as reaching closer to 60%. Liposomes achieve this by encasing NAD+ in a phosphatidylcholine bilayer — essentially the same material human cell membranes are built from — which protects the molecule from stomach acid and digestive enzymes long enough to reach circulation intact. DeLauer contrasts this direct-delivery approach with precursor supplements like NR or NMN, which require the body to enzymatically convert them into NAD+, a step he argues introduces inefficiency and caps how much benefit precursors alone can provide. Mitochondria and Cellular Energy NAD+'s role as an electron carrier in the mitochondrial electron transport chain is the mechanistic backbone for the energy claims in the video. DeLauer frames restored NAD+ availability as supporting ATP production broadly, positioning it as acting further upstream than more familiar energy supplements like CoQ10 or creatine, which support specific downstream processes rather than the cofactor pool itself. The argument is that addressing fatigue at the mitochondrial-cofactor level is more foundational than stimulant-based approaches, though the video is clear this works alongside — not instead of — sleep, training, and diet. DNA Repair and PARP Enzymes A significant portion of the mechanistic case rests on DNA repair. PARP1, the enzyme activated by DNA damage, can consume up to 80% of the nuclear NAD+ pool to fuel repair, and NAD+ depletion has been linked to roughly a 40% reduction in repair rates — creating a feedback loop where low NAD+ both causes and worsens genomic instability. DeLauer uses this to elevate the conversation beyond "energy supplement" into genomic maintenance, and notes that PARPs and sirtuins compete for the same limited NAD+ pool, which becomes the bridge into the video's longevity-pathway discussion. Sirtuins and Longevity Pathways Sirtuins, especially SIRT1, require NAD+ as a direct co-substrate — without it, sirtuin activators like resveratrol have no mechanism to work through. DeLauer explains that resveratrol functions as an allosteric activator, boosting SIRT1's catalytic efficiency for whatever NAD+ is available, rather than substituting for NAD+ itself. This is used to argue that NAD+ restoration and sirtuin activators are complementary strategies, and sirtuins are described as a "master switch" connecting metabolism, inflammation, and cellular aging — a useful simplification, though human trial evidence for sirtuin-pathway longevity benefits remains far more limited than the cell and animal data it's based on. Practical Dosing and Stacking The featured product, Rho Nutrition's Liposomal NAD+, is dosed at about 4ml daily (roughly 100mg of NAD+), in a vegan, sugar-free, lemon-flavored liquid sized for about 30 servings per bottle. The core consumer pitch is consolidation — replacing a cabinet of separate energy, antioxidant, and longevity pills with one liquid — which is as much a convenience argument as a biochemical one. It's worth noting this segment is a paid partnership promoted with the discount code DELAUER20; the underlying NAD+ and liposomal-delivery science is grounded in published research, but the specific "replaces your entire cabinet" framing is sponsored marketing language layered on top of it. 1 Don't wait for symptoms NAD+ declines roughly 50% between age 20 and 60 on a fairly predictable curve — if you're considering support, earlier maintenance is the framing DeLauer uses, not waiting until fatigue or recovery issues show up. 2 Compare absorption, not just dose When shopping for NAD+ or precursor products, check for bioavailability data. Standard capsules land around 10–20% absorption; liposomal liquids are marketed toward 60% — that gap matters more than milligrams on the label. 3 Reassess NR/NMN if you've seen no effect Precursors require enzymatic conversion and face rapid CD38/PARP consumption plus homeostatic feedback. If you've taken NR or NMN without noticeable results, this conversion bottleneck is a plausible reason, not necessarily a sign NAD+ support doesn't work for you. 4 Pair with a sirtuin activator deliberately If longevity signaling is the goal, resveratrol (or similar) only works when NAD+ is available as substrate. Taking a sirtuin activator alone, without addressing NAD+ levels, has little to act on. 5 Watch for high DNA-repair-demand periods Heavy sun exposure, intense training blocks, or illness spike PARP activity, which competes with sirtuins for the same NAD+ pool. Build in recovery periods rather than assuming supplementation alone offsets sustained high-damage stress. 6 Take liquid liposomal NAD+ on an empty stomach Liposomal delivery is generally recommended away from heavy meals to reduce competition for absorption pathways — a practical detail worth applying if you try a liquid liposomal format. 7 Weigh consolidation against cost A single daily 4ml serving replacing multiple pills is a convenience win, but price-per-serving on liposomal liquids is typically higher than buying individual, cheaper components separately — factor that into the "replaces your cabinet" pitch. 8 Discount the marketing framing, not the mechanism "Replaces your entire supplement cabinet" is sponsored language. The NAD+/PARP/sirtuin biochemistry behind it is real and published — evaluate the science and the sales pitch separately. 9 Check for third-party testing Before trusting a liposomal NAD+ brand's absorption or purity claims, look for independent lab verification (COAs) rather than relying on the manufacturer's marketing copy alone. 10 Track subjective measures over 4–6 weeks Energy, recovery, and sleep quality are the practical signals to monitor if you trial NAD+ supplementation — human longevity outcomes take years to measure, but short-term subjective changes are the realistic feedback loop available to you. This mind map summarizes and contextualizes publicly available information about the video and related published research on NAD+ biology. It is not medical advice, and the featured product segment is a paid sponsorship.

title: Thomas DeLauer – 1 Scoop Fades Wrinkles, Brightens Skin & Reverses Biological Age
text: Thomas DeLauer – 1 Scoop Fades Wrinkles, Brightens Skin & Reverses Biological Age 1 Scoop Fades Wrinkles, Brightens Skin Reverses Biological Age Thomas DeLauer · 2026-06-11 · Skin Health, Collagen Anti-Aging 🗺 Mind Map 📄 Full Summary ⚡ Actionable Takeaways Collagen Peptides: What They Are How They Work ▶ 🧬 What Is Collagen? ▶ Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, making up roughly 30% of total protein content. It provides the structural scaffold for skin, joints, tendons, ligaments, and bones. Type I collagen dominates in skin — it forms dense fibres that give skin its tensile strength and smooth appearance. Type II is primarily found in cartilage, and Type III is abundant in skin alongside Type I. 📉 Why Collagen Declines With Age ▶ The body's ability to produce collagen declines at roughly 1% per year after age 25. By age 40, skin collagen density has measurably decreased; by age 60, it may be reduced by 30–40%. Contributing factors include UV exposure (which degrades existing collagen fibres), chronic inflammation, high sugar intake (which causes glycation — cross-linking that stiffens collagen fibres), and declining oestrogen in women after menopause. 💊 How Collagen Peptides Differ from Whole Collagen ▶ Collagen peptides (also called hydrolysed collagen) are collagen proteins broken down into shorter chains of amino acids through enzymatic hydrolysis. This process dramatically improves bioavailability — rather than being digested into random amino acids, specific bioactive peptides (dipeptides and tripeptides) survive digestion and are absorbed intact. These peptides then signal fibroblast cells in the dermis to produce new collagen, elastin, and hyaluronic acid. 🔬 The Clinical Evidence Base ▶ A 2025 study published in npj Aging demonstrated that a collagen amino acid composition supplement reduced participants' biological age by an average of 1.4 years over six months. Multiple independent randomised controlled trials have also shown oral collagen peptides improve skin hydration, increase elasticity, and reduce the appearance of wrinkles within 8–12 weeks of consistent daily supplementation. ⚗ Key Amino Acids: Glycine, Proline, Hydroxyproline ▶ Collagen peptides are uniquely rich in glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline — amino acids rarely found in high concentrations in other dietary proteins. Glycine is also a precursor to glutathione (the body's master antioxidant) and plays a role in sleep quality and metabolic regulation. Hydroxyproline tripeptides specifically signal fibroblasts to upregulate collagen synthesis in the dermis. Biological Age vs Chronological Age ▶ ⏰ What Is Biological Age? ▶ Biological age is a measure of how old your cells and tissues function, as distinct from your chronological age. It is typically measured using epigenetic clocks — algorithms that analyse DNA methylation patterns at specific sites across the genome. These patterns change in predictable ways as we age, and lifestyle interventions can meaningfully shift them in either direction. 🧪 Epigenetic Clocks: How Biological Age Is Measured ▶ Epigenetic clocks like Horvath's clock, PhenoAge, and GrimAge measure the degree of methylation at specific CpG sites across the genome. Younger biological age profiles correlate with better health outcomes, lower disease risk, and longer lifespan. The exciting finding in the 2025 collagen study was that a simple daily supplement produced a measurable shift in these clock readings within six months. 🔄 Can You Reverse Biological Age? ▶ Multiple interventions have now been shown to reduce biological age as measured by epigenetic clocks: caloric restriction, consistent exercise, quality sleep, stress management, and certain nutritional interventions including collagen peptides. DeLauer emphasises that biological age reversal is not theoretical — it is now measurable at the molecular level, though results depend on consistency and the combination of interventions used. 📊 The Collagen–Biological Age Connection ▶ The 2025 npj Aging study found that a collagen amino acid formulation reduced biological age by 1.4 years on average after six months — a clinically meaningful shift achieved through a single daily supplement. DeLauer contextualises this within the broader longevity framework: reducing biological age by even one to two years could translate to meaningfully lower risk of age-related disease over time. Wrinkle Reduction Skin Rejuvenation ▶ 🪞 How Wrinkles Form ▶ Wrinkles form through a combination of collagen degradation, elastin breakdown, declining hyaluronic acid production, and repetitive facial muscle contractions. As the dermis thins with age, the skin loses its ability to bounce back from compression — creases deepen and become permanent. UV radiation accelerates this process by activating matrix metalloproteinase enzymes that break down collagen fibres in the dermis. ✨ How Collagen Peptides Reduce Wrinkles ▶ Oral collagen peptides reach the dermis intact, where they bind to fibroblast receptors and upregulate production of new collagen (Types I and III), elastin, and hyaluronic acid. Multiple RCTs show measurable improvements in skin elasticity and significant reductions in eye corner wrinkle depth after 8–12 weeks. The mechanism is not simply adding collagen but triggering the skin's own regenerative processes. 💧 Skin Hydration Hyaluronic Acid ▶ Collagen peptide supplementation has been shown to increase skin hydration — partly through the direct effects of glycine and proline on the skin barrier, and partly through upregulation of hyaluronic acid synthase. Hyaluronic acid holds up to 1000 times its weight in water, and its production declines sharply with age. Higher dermal hydration plumps the skin, making wrinkles less visible and the skin surface more reflective (contributing to perceived brightness). 🌟 Skin Brightening Mechanisms ▶ Skin brightness is driven by both structural and biochemical factors. Increased hydration plumps the dermis and improves light reflection. Glycine as a glutathione precursor helps reduce oxidative stress and may attenuate UV-induced hyperpigmentation. Better collagen density reduces the irregular light scattering caused by degraded collagen networks — giving skin a more uniform, luminous appearance without topical cosmetics. Skin Hydration Elasticity Science ▶ 🧴 Why Topical Collagen Doesn't Work ▶ Topical collagen creams are largely ineffective because collagen molecules are too large to penetrate the skin barrier — they sit on the surface and create a temporary film effect but do not reach the dermis where new collagen synthesis occurs. DeLauer contrasts this with oral collagen peptides, which are absorbed through the gut, circulate in the bloodstream, and are specifically taken up by fibroblasts in the dermis. ⚡ Elastin: The Bounce-Back Protein ▶ Elastin gives skin its elasticity — the ability to stretch and snap back. Elastin production essentially ceases after puberty, so the body relies on maintaining existing elastin fibres. Collagen peptide supplementation has been shown to upregulate both collagen and elastin synthesis in fibroblasts simultaneously, improving skin elasticity scores in clinical trials within 12 weeks of supplementation. 📐 Measuring Skin Elasticity ▶ Skin elasticity is measured using cutometers — devices that apply suction to skin and measure how quickly it rebounds. Studies using collagen peptide supplementation consistently show significant improvements in cutometer readings after 8–12 weeks. DeLauer notes that these measurements are objective and reproducible, making them reliable evidence of structural skin improvement rather than subjective perception. 🔋 Optimal Dosing Timing ▶ Most research on skin outcomes uses 5–10g of hydrolysed collagen peptides per day. DeLauer notes that Vitamin C is essential for collagen synthesis — without adequate Vitamin C, the body cannot hydroxylate proline into hydroxyproline, a critical step in collagen formation. Taking collagen with a Vitamin C source (or a supplement containing both) maximises the biological yield from supplementation. Morning or post-exercise timing may improve uptake. The Gut–Skin Axis ▶ 🔗 How Gut Health Affects Skin ▶ The gut–skin axis describes the bidirectional communication between the gastrointestinal microbiome and skin health. A disrupted gut microbiome increases intestinal permeability, allowing inflammatory bacterial products to circulate systemically — triggering skin inflammation, accelerating collagen degradation, and worsening conditions like acne, eczema, and rosacea. Healing the gut often produces visible skin improvements. 🦠 Gut Microbiome Collagen Production ▶ Beneficial gut bacteria produce short-chain fatty acids that reduce systemic inflammation — directly protecting collagen fibres from inflammatory degradation. Some species also produce enzymes that improve the bioavailability of ingested collagen peptides. DeLauer argues that optimising the gut microbiome (through fibre, fermented foods, and reduced UPFs) compounds the benefits of collagen supplementation. 🥗 Dietary Foundations for Skin Health ▶ Beyond collagen peptides, DeLauer highlights dietary patterns that preserve skin collagen: eating adequate protein (the amino acid pool from whole foods supports collagen synthesis), consuming polyphenol-rich foods (berries, dark chocolate, green tea) that inhibit collagen-degrading enzymes, and minimising dietary sugar (which glycates and stiffens collagen through the Maillard reaction, accelerating visible aging). 😴 Sleep Skin Regeneration ▶ Deep sleep (slow-wave sleep) is when the body performs the majority of its collagen repair and synthesis. Growth hormone — released in pulses during deep sleep — directly stimulates fibroblast activity and collagen production. DeLauer emphasises that even optimal supplementation produces diminished returns without adequate sleep: 7–9 hours in a cool, dark environment is a non-negotiable foundation for skin regeneration. Anti-Aging Lifestyle Stack ▶ 🏋 Exercise Collagen Synthesis ▶ Resistance training stimulates collagen synthesis in both skin and connective tissue by increasing mechanical tension on fibroblasts. Studies show that taking collagen peptides 30–60 minutes before exercise may further enhance collagen synthesis in tendons and skin by providing available amino acids during the post-exercise anabolic window. DeLauer advocates pairing supplementation with consistent strength training for maximal anti-aging results. ☀ UV Protection as Priority One ▶ UV radiation is the single largest environmental driver of skin aging — responsible for up to 80% of visible facial aging. UVA rays penetrate deep into the dermis and activate matrix metalloproteinases that destroy collagen and elastin fibres. DeLauer stresses that supplementation works best when combined with consistent daily SPF 30+ application, making sun protection the most cost-effective anti-aging intervention available. 🚫 Collagen Destroyers to Eliminate ▶ Several lifestyle factors actively accelerate collagen destruction: smoking (carbon monoxide and free radicals directly break down collagen fibres), excess sugar intake (glycation cross-links and stiffens collagen), chronic stress (cortisol degrades collagen and thins skin over time), and alcohol (dehydrates skin and generates oxidative stress that damages collagen networks). Reducing these factors has a compounding effect with supplementation. 🌊 Hydration Skin Barrier Function ▶ Adequate water intake (typically 2–3 litres per day depending on body size and activity) maintains the turgor pressure that keeps skin plump and elastic. DeLauer notes that electrolytes — particularly sodium and potassium — are necessary for water to be effectively retained intracellularly. A well-hydrated skin barrier is more resistant to environmental damage and supports faster collagen repair after UV or mechanical stress. Collagen Peptides: The Science Behind the Supplement Thomas DeLauer opens by distinguishing collagen peptides (hydrolysed collagen) from whole collagen protein, explaining that enzymatic hydrolysis breaks collagen into short bioactive chains — dipeptides and tripeptides — that survive digestion and are absorbed intact into the bloodstream. These peptides then travel to the dermis, where they bind to fibroblast receptors and signal the body to upregulate production of new collagen (Types I and III), elastin, and hyaluronic acid. This is fundamentally different from eating more protein: specific collagen peptides carry a unique signalling function that general amino acids cannot replicate. He points to a 2025 study published in npj Aging demonstrating that a collagen amino acid formulation reduced biological age by an average of 1.4 years in six months — one of the more striking recent findings in the anti-aging nutrition space. Biological Age vs Chronological Age DeLauer dedicates significant time to explaining biological age — a measure of how old your cells function, distinct from your birth year. Biological age is now measurable using epigenetic clocks (algorithms like PhenoAge and GrimAge) that analyse DNA methylation patterns at specific genomic sites. Multiple interventions have been shown to reduce biological age as measured by these clocks: caloric restriction, consistent exercise, sleep optimisation, and certain nutritional interventions. The collagen study finding of 1.4 years of biological age reduction in six months is framed by DeLauer as evidence that targeted supplementation can meaningfully shift these markers — though he emphasises this works best in the context of an overall health-conscious lifestyle. Wrinkle Reduction: Mechanisms and Evidence Wrinkles form as collagen and elastin break down with age, UV exposure, smoking, and sugar-induced glycation. The dermis thins, loses its structural scaffold, and can no longer support the skin surface uniformly. DeLauer explains that topical collagen creams cannot penetrate the skin barrier — the collagen molecule is simply too large. Oral collagen peptides bypass this problem by being absorbed through the gut, circulating in the blood, and being actively taken up by dermal fibroblasts. Multiple independent randomised controlled trials show significant reductions in wrinkle depth and improvements in skin elasticity after 8–12 weeks of 5–10g daily supplementation. The effect size is meaningful rather than cosmetic — cutometer measurements show objective improvements in skin biomechanics. Skin Hydration, Hyaluronic Acid, and Brightness Oral collagen peptides improve skin hydration through two mechanisms: the amino acids (especially glycine and proline) directly support the skin barrier, and collagen peptides upregulate hyaluronic acid synthase — the enzyme that produces hyaluronic acid in the dermis. Hyaluronic acid holds up to 1000 times its weight in water, and its production declines sharply with age. Greater dermal hydration plumps the skin visibly, making wrinkles less deep and the skin surface more reflective. Glycine also serves as a precursor to glutathione, the body's master antioxidant, potentially attenuating UV-induced hyperpigmentation and contributing to the brightening effect DeLauer describes. The Gut–Skin Axis DeLauer explores how gut health profoundly affects skin outcomes through what researchers call the gut–skin axis. A disrupted microbiome increases intestinal permeability, allowing inflammatory bacterial products to circulate systemically — triggering skin inflammation, accelerating collagen degradation, and worsening inflammatory skin conditions. Beneficial gut bacteria produce short-chain fatty acids that reduce systemic inflammation, directly protecting collagen from inflammatory breakdown. DeLauer argues that optimising the gut through fibre-rich foods, fermented foods, and reduced ultra-processed food intake compounds the benefits of collagen supplementation significantly. The Anti-Aging Lifestyle Stack DeLauer contextualises collagen supplementation within a broader anti-aging lifestyle framework. Daily SPF 30+ application is described as the single most impactful anti-aging intervention, since UV radiation accounts for up to 80% of visible facial aging. Resistance training stimulates fibroblast activity and collagen synthesis through mechanical tension. Deep sleep (7–9 hours) is when growth hormone-driven collagen repair peaks. Eliminating or reducing collagen destroyers — smoking, dietary sugar, chronic stress, and excess alcohol — has a compounding protective effect. The key message is that collagen supplementation is most effective as part of a comprehensive strategy, not as a standalone fix. 01 Take 5–10g of hydrolysed collagen peptides daily, consistently, for at least 8–12 weeks. Skin and biological age benefits require sustained supplementation — short-term or sporadic use won't produce the same results seen in clinical trials. 02 Always pair collagen with Vitamin C — either from food (citrus, bell peppers, kiwi) or a supplement. Vitamin C is required for the hydroxylation of proline into hydroxyproline, which is essential for collagen fibre formation in the dermis. 03 Apply SPF 30+ sunscreen every day, including in winter and on cloudy days. UV radiation accounts for up to 80% of visible facial aging — sunscreen is the most cost-effective anti-aging intervention available and nothing else comes close in impact. 04 Try taking collagen peptides 30–60 minutes before resistance training. The combination of available collagen peptides and the mechanical stimulus of exercise may enhance collagen synthesis in both skin and connective tissue beyond either intervention alone. 05 Significantly reduce added sugar intake. Sugar glycates collagen fibres — cross-linking them in a way that makes them stiff, disorganised, and unable to provide the skin support that prevents wringles. This process is called the Maillard reaction and it accelerates visible aging measurably. 06 Stop (or significantly cut) smoking. Cigarette smoke directly breaks down collagen and elastin fibres through free radical damage and carbon monoxide-mediated hypoxia in the dermis — the impact on visible skin aging is dramatic and among the most reversible once you stop. 07 Prioritise 7–9 hours of quality sleep each night. Deep (slow-wave) sleep is when growth hormone is released and drives the majority of collagen repair and synthesis. Poor sleep undermines any supplementation protocol you adopt. 08 Eat a polyphenol-rich diet: dark berries, green tea, dark chocolate, red onion, and turmeric. Polyphenols inhibit matrix metalloproteinase enzymes — the enzymes that break down collagen in the dermis — giving existing collagen fibres a longer functional lifespan. 09 Feed your gut microbiome to support the gut–skin axis: eat diverse plant fibre, fermented foods (kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi), and reduce ultra-processed foods. A healthy microbiome reduces the systemic inflammation that accelerates collagen degradation throughout the body. 10 Don't rely on topical collagen creams for structural improvement — collagen molecules cannot penetrate the skin barrier. Invest in oral hydrolysed collagen peptides and foundational lifestyle habits instead; these are where the clinical evidence is strongest.

title: REGROW Stem Cells & Burn Stubborn Fat — Thomas DeLauer
text: REGROW Stem Cells & Burn Stubborn Fat — Thomas DeLauer Thomas DeLauer Most People Never Do This! REGROW Stem Cells Burn Stubborn Fat In 24 Hours Thomas DeLauer Watch on YouTube Mind Map Full Summary Actionable Takeaways 1 The Core Switch: Sugar Fat One Switch, Two Outcomes + DeLauer frames the entire video around a single metabolic flip: when cells stop burning glucose and start burning fatty acids, two things happen on the same pathway at once — stem cells become more regenerative, and the body burns fat to make it happen. It isn't two separate systems; it's one switch producing two payoffs. Grid Power vs. Generator + Running on sugar is like a house on grid power — easy, lazy, the body coasts. Forcing the body onto fat is like switching to its own generator: different "repair crews" clock in, and the fuel being burned is the very fat you've been trying to lose. Why It's Kept Hidden + DeLauer argues an entire industry — stem cell clinics, peptide sellers, IV drips, longevity memberships costing hundreds of thousands a year — profits from making this switch sound complicated and expensive, when the actual levers are free and ordinary. How Fast It Flips + In animal studies, this switch begins flipping within hours, not weeks, and not through a cabinet full of supplements. The research suggests the body starts behaving like a younger version of itself: burning fat better and repairing cells better. Ranking the Five Levers + DeLauer ranks five habits from weakest to strongest evidence and impact: sauna (5), resistant starch (4), cold exposure (3), high-intensity intervals (2), and fasting (1) — the free habit he says triggers the strongest response of all. 2 Lever #5: Sauna Heat Exposure The Lipolytic Hormone Pulse + Heat stress drives a release of noradrenaline and a pulse of growth hormone, both lipolytic — they signal fat cells to release stored fatty acids into the blood. DeLauer compares it to doing low-grade cardio while just sitting still. Heat Shock Proteins Progenitor Cells + The regeneration data here is early and largely petri-dish work, but it shows heat shock proteins nudging progenitor cells. DeLauer is upfront that this isn't yet human-confirmed, but the heat-triggered regenerative pathway is real in lab models. "Revving in Neutral" — The Catch + Sauna mobilizes fat out of storage, but mobilizing isn't the same as burning. If those freed fatty acids aren't used, they go right back into storage — so sauna alone, without something burning the fuel, doesn't reliably strip fat. Muscle Preservation, Not Standalone Fat Loss + Where sauna does show real benefit is in preserving muscle and supporting growth hormone, plus strong Finnish/Nordic evidence for cardiovascular and recovery benefits. DeLauer calls it a "multiplier" that amplifies habits already working, not a centerpiece. Protocol + 175 200 F for 15 20 minutes. If time allows, do it as intervals: 15 minutes hot, step out a couple minutes, repeat. The heating-and-cooling cycle is what drives the heat-shock-protein adaptation. Stay hydrated. 3 Lever #4: Resistant Starch Gut Stem Cells What Resistant Starch Actually Is + Unlike most starches, resistant starch passes through the small intestine undigested and travels intact to the colon, where it feeds gut bacteria — functioning more like fiber than a typical carbohydrate. Nature Metabolism: 2.8 kg in 8 Weeks + DeLauer cites a Nature Metabolism study where 8 weeks of resistant starch helped people with excess weight lose an average of 2.8 kg (about 6 lbs) and improved insulin resistance — some of the strongest human fat-loss data in the whole video. British Journal of Nutrition: 60% More Gut Stem Cells + A human study found resistant starch increased proliferation of cells in the gut crypts — where intestinal stem cells live — by about 60% in adults over 50, a rare case of human (not just petri-dish) stem cell evidence. Cook, Cool, (Reheat) + A hot, fresh potato has little resistant starch — it forms when starches are cooked and then cooled, ideally for 12 hours. Reheating gently only costs about 15 20% of the benefit, so warmed leftovers still work well. Best Sources Pairing + Cooked-and-cooled potatoes, rice, beans, green bananas, and oats all work — introduce them slowly to avoid bloating. DeLauer pairs this habit with a targeted probiotic (his sponsor, Seed) designed to survive stomach acid and colonize the colon. 4 Lever #3: Cold Exposure Brown Fat White Fat vs. Brown Fat + White fat stores energy; brown fat burns it for heat. DeLauer's focus isn't the well-worn "cold plunge" story but what cold specifically does to convert fat-precursor cells toward the brown, calorie-burning type. Cold Pushes Precursor Cells Toward Brown Fat + Petri-dish work suggests cold pushes fat precursor (stem) cells to differentiate into brown, calorie-burning fat rather than storage-type white fat — effectively building a bigger internal "wood stove" over time. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology Finding + People with active brown fat burned about 15% more calories after short-term cold exposure than people without it — real evidence, though DeLauer notes rodent studies also showed animals eating more afterward, offsetting fat loss. The Hunger Catch + Cold exposure can temporarily spike metabolic rate 90 350%, which is exactly why people feel ravenous after a cold pool or plunge. The risk is overeating right afterward and erasing the deficit the cold created. Protocol + 50 59 F for just a couple of minutes is enough — colder isn't better. Critically, let the body warm up naturally afterward instead of immediately eating breakfast; that natural rewarming is what helps convert white fat to brown fat. 5 Lever #2: High-Intensity Intervals Mobilized, Not Created + Going truly hard mobilizes hematopoietic stem cells that already live in bone marrow out into the bloodstream — it's not growing new stem cells from scratch, but releasing existing reserves, which DeLauer likens to flushing a back-room stockpile onto the main floor. Intensity-Dependent CD34 Release + Researchers found the mobilization effect is intensity dependent: a short, vigorous bout pushed more CD34+ stem cells into circulation than a longer, easier session — favoring hard, brief efforts over long moderate ones. Catecholamine Surge Afterburn + Hard bursts trigger a catecholamine surge that drives lipolysis. Matched-workout studies show intervals produce more afterburn and fat oxidation in the hours afterward than steady-state cardio. Recovery Is the Real Bottleneck + Going all-out daily or every other day spikes cortisol, tanks recovery, and blunts the very benefits being chased. Mobilized stem cells still need protein and rest to be "actualized" — the interval is the stimulus, recovery is where the adaptation happens. Protocol + Two sessions per week: either a Norwegian 4x4 (4 minutes all-out, 3 minutes easy, repeated 4 times) or eight 30-second all-out sprints on a bike, rower, or uphill run. Doing intervals at the end of a fasted window compounds the fat-burning effect. 6 Lever #1: Fasting — The Strongest Response 24-Hour Fast Doubles Intestinal Stem Cell Regeneration + A study published in Cell Stem Cell found a 24-hour fast doubled the regenerative capacity of intestinal stem cells — the cells that rebuild gut lining — in both young and old mice. DeLauer is candid that this is rodent data, but calls doubling "doubling." The Same Switch, Hit Hardest + Researchers pinpointed the mechanism: when the body stops eating, cells switch from burning carbohydrate to burning fatty acids, and that same fat-burning switch is what tells stem cells to regenerate. They reproduced the effect with a molecule that flips the switch without fasting. The Refeeding Window Matters More + A 2024 MIT follow-up found the regeneration surge is actually strongest during refeeding right after a fast — but that same rebound can also spike mTOR in less desirable ways, so how you break a fast (clean protein, avoiding highly insulinogenic foods) matters as much as the fast itself. Kitchen Analogy: Closing to Clean + DeLauer compares constant eating to a kitchen that never closes — cooks working nonstop, nothing ever cleaned. Fasting closes the kitchen so the "cleanup crew" (cellular repair and regeneration processes) can finally come in and rebuild. Protocol + Beginners: start with a 16-hour overnight fasting window. Build gradually toward a full 24-hour fast, aiming for twice a week once adapted — not daily. The metabolic sugar-to-fat flip is already underway within the first 24 hours. The Core Switch DeLauer opens with a central claim: a single metabolic switch controls both cellular repair and fat metabolism at once, and for most people it's flipped off. That switch is the shift from burning glucose to burning fatty acids. When cells make that shift, two things happen on the same pathway simultaneously — stem cells become more regenerative, and the body burns fat to power the process. He frames the wellness and longevity industry (stem cell clinics, peptides, IV drips, expensive longevity memberships) as having a financial incentive to make this sound complicated, when the actual levers — how you eat, how warm you keep yourself, how hard you push physically, and what you feed your gut bacteria — are ordinary and free. Animal studies suggest the switch can begin flipping within hours rather than weeks. Sauna and Heat Exposure Ranked fifth and weakest of the five habits, sauna use triggers a release of noradrenaline and growth hormone that signals fat cells to release stored fatty acids — comparable to low-grade cardio while sitting still. Early, largely petri-dish research suggests heat shock proteins may also nudge progenitor cells toward regeneration, though DeLauer is careful to flag this evidence as preliminary. The key caveat is that sauna mobilizes fat without necessarily burning it; freed fatty acids can simply return to storage unless something else in the routine actually uses them as fuel. Where sauna shows the strongest evidence is in muscle preservation, growth hormone support, and cardiovascular/recovery benefits backed by Finnish and Nordic research. He recommends 175 200 F for 15 20 minutes, ideally as heat-and-cool intervals, positioning sauna as a multiplier layered onto habits that are already working rather than a standalone fat-loss tool. Resistant Starch and Gut Stem Cells Fourth on the list, resistant starch is starch that survives digestion in the small intestine and reaches the colon intact, feeding gut bacteria. DeLauer cites a Nature Metabolism study in which 8 weeks of resistant starch intake led to an average 2.8 kg fat loss and improved insulin resistance in people carrying excess weight — among the strongest human data referenced in the video. A separate study in the British Journal of Nutrition found resistant starch increased proliferation of intestinal stem cells in the gut crypts by roughly 60% in adults over 50, one of the few human (rather than lab-dish) findings on stem cells in the episode. The practical method is to cook starchy foods like potatoes, rice, or beans, then cool them in the fridge for several hours (ideally 12) before eating, since resistant starch forms during cooling and only modestly degrades on reheating. He pairs the habit with a colon-targeted probiotic. Cold Exposure and Brown Fat Ranked third, cold exposure's newer angle isn't the familiar "cold plunge boosts willpower" story but its effect on brown fat — the metabolically active tissue that burns energy for heat, as opposed to white fat, which stores it. Research cited in the Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism found people with active brown fat burned about 15% more calories after short-term cold exposure, and lab-dish work suggests cold nudges fat precursor cells to differentiate into brown fat rather than white fat over time. The major catch is a sharp, temporary spike in metabolic rate (cited as 90 350% in some studies) that drives significant post-exposure hunger, making overeating easy. DeLauer's protocol is modest cold — 50 to 59 F for just a couple of minutes — followed by letting the body rewarm naturally rather than immediately eating, which he says is the step most people skip. High-Intensity Intervals Second on the list, hard interval training mobilizes hematopoietic stem cells already stored in bone marrow into the bloodstream — not creating new stem cells, but releasing existing reserves, an effect shown to be intensity-dependent, with shorter and harder efforts mobilizing more CD34+ cells than longer, easier sessions. On the fat-loss side, intervals trigger a catecholamine surge that drives lipolysis and produces more afterburn and fat oxidation in the hours after training than steady-state cardio. DeLauer cautions that more is not better: daily or near-daily all-out efforts spike cortisol and blunt recovery, undermining the benefits. His recommended protocol is two sessions per week — either a Norwegian 4x4 (four rounds of four minutes hard, three minutes easy) or eight 30-second all-out sprints — with the effect compounding when performed at the end of a fasted window. Fasting: The Strongest Lever Fasting tops DeLauer's ranking as the habit that flips the sugar-to-fat switch hardest. He cites a study published in Cell Stem Cell showing a 24-hour fast doubled the regenerative capacity of intestinal stem cells in both young and old mice, with researchers tracing the mechanism to the same carbohydrate-to-fatty-acid metabolic shift discussed throughout the video — they even replicated the regenerative effect using a molecule that triggers the switch without fasting at all. A 2024 MIT follow-up added an important nuance: the regeneration surge is actually strongest during the refeeding window immediately after a fast, meaning how a fast is broken (clean protein, avoiding highly insulinogenic foods) matters nearly as much as the fast itself, since the same rebound can spike mTOR in less favorable ways. DeLauer's suggested progression is a 16-hour overnight fast for beginners, building gradually to a full 24-hour fast performed around twice a week rather than daily. 1 Think of these five habits as one lever, not five separate hacks — every one of them works by driving the same sugar-to-fat metabolic switch. 2 If you're new to fasting, start with a 16-hour overnight window; build gradually toward a full 24-hour fast about twice a week rather than daily. 3 Don't chase a fast with a big insulin-spiking meal — the regeneration surge peaks during refeeding, so break your fast with clean protein, not sugar. 4 Do two high-intensity interval sessions a week: a Norwegian 4x4 (4 min hard / 3 min easy x4) or eight 30-second all-out sprints. 5 Stack your interval session onto the tail end of a fasted window — the fat-burning effects of each compound the other. 6 Finish showers with 2 3 minutes of cold water at 50 59 F, then let your body rewarm on its own instead of dressing warm or eating right away. 7 Cook potatoes, rice, or beans and refrigerate them for at least a few hours (ideally 12) before eating to convert the starch into gut-feeding resistant starch. 8 Use sauna as a recovery multiplier, not a fat-loss centerpiece — 175 200 F for 15 20 minutes, ideally in heat/cool intervals after training. 9 Cap hard interval training at two sessions per week — pushing all-out daily spikes cortisol and blunts the very stem cell and fat-loss benefits you're after. 10 Layer the habits in over 30 days instead of all at once: fasting first, then intervals, then cold exposure, then resistant starch, then sauna as the finishing touch.
